reconcile.connective: Defenders distinguish scope and sense: Genesis forbids only another universal water-deluge, while Nahum's "flood" is a local, figurative judgment on one city.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (Steve Wells) presses the objection directly, reading Nahum 1:8's "overrunning flood" as God again destroying everything by water against the Genesis 9 promise.

excerpts.excerpt_text: not a general deluge, otherwise notwithstanding this promise there might be, as there have been, particular inundations, which have overflowed particular countries and places, but not the whole earth …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly limits the Gen 9 promise to a universal deluge, explicitly allowing local inundations — the core scope harmonization against Nahum's local flood.

excerpts.excerpt_text: This promise does not prohibit worldwide judgment, but it restricts the means by which God will do it (see 2 Pet 3:4-13).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States the promise restricts the means (water-deluge), not all judgment — squarely on the tension with Nahum's judgment-flood.

excerpts.excerpt_text: with an overrunning flood—that is, with irresistible might which overruns every barrier like a flood. This image is often applied to overwhelming armies of invaders.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Reads Nahum's flood as a metaphor for an invading army against one city, dissolving the apparent conflict with the literal-water Genesis promise.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Genesis 9:11 and Nahum 1:8
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats both passages directly: the Genesis promise excludes only a general deluge (allowing particular inundations), and Nahum's flood is the Medo-Babylonian army 'like a flood' (or the literal river breach) against Nineveh alone.
